objects: AUC; absolute disease risk; risk prediction
assumptions: Evaluation of prediction models for clinically meaningful absolute risks
conclusion: AUC alone does not describe absolute disease risks and motivates complementary prediction indices.
scope: Motivation for the unified evaluation framework
span: Despite its widespread use, the ROC curve and AUC are not without limitations and they are not the only ways to assess the performance of a prediction model. For instance, it has been pointed out that that the AUC is not directly related to the absolute disease risks (i.e. probability of disease given test result), which is often of great clinical interest [6], [7].

objects: Latent liability; disease indicator; liability threshold
assumptions: Normal latent liability; affected status defined by threshold exceedance
conclusion: The framework models binary disease as an underlying normally distributed liability exceeding a threshold.
span: The framework is based on the liability threshold model, which assumes an underlying liability that is normally distributed. Affected individuals have a liability above the threshold.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | Introduction

objects: Measurable liability z; total liability; Vm
assumptions: Known risk factors define the measurable component of liability
conclusion: Measurable liability is normal with mean zero and variance explained by known variants, and total liability conditional on z is normal with mean z.
scope: Population and conditional liability distributions; source equation images are not reconstructed
span: The measurable liability is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance equal to the total variance (or heritability) explained by the known variants (). The overall liability conditioned on the measurable liability (z) is normally distributed with mean z and variance 1−. Vm and are used interchangeably in this paper, with the former usually referring to the concept of variance explained and the latter referring to its level.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | The liability threshold model

objects: Population outcome probability K; variance explained Vm
assumptions: Overall outcome probability and variance explained are known
conclusion: The framework takes population outcome probability and variance explained as inputs and can be applied to case-control studies when both are known.
scope: Aggregate inputs; case-control applicability does not substitute sampled case fraction for population probability
span: The methodology described here can be applied to case-control studies, as long as the overall probability of outcome and variance explained are known. By supplying the overall disease probability, the appropriate absolute risks and reclassification indices can be computed.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | Discussion

objects: Risk distribution; AUC; discrimination slope; reclassification improvement; high-risk case proportion
assumptions: Liability-threshold variance-explained framework with specified K and Vm
conclusion: The framework derives the risk distribution and multiple predictive indices from population disease probability and total variance explained.
scope: Analytic model-implied quantities; no claim of fitted posterior inference
span: The distribution of predicted risks in the population can be derived analytically given the overall probability of disease and the variance explained. We can also compute many indices of predictive power, such as AUC, discrimination slope, reclassification improvement and the proportion of cases explained by specific percentile of population at the highest risk.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | Discussion

objects: Sensitivity; specificity; percentile cut-offs; area under ROC
assumptions: Classification by measurable-liability percentile; model-implied probabilities
conclusion: The main AUC calculation evaluates sensitivity and specificity over 5000 percentile cut-offs and estimates the area under the resulting ROC curve.
scope: Numerical evaluation of analytic prediction quantities
span: The other cells in the 2×2 table are computed readily given Pr(TP). Sensitivity and specificity are calculated using 5000 percentile cut-offs. Area under the curve (AUC) is then estimated from the graph using the R function integrate.xy from the sfsmisc package.

objects: Conditional liability mean and variance; AUC
assumptions: Conditioning measurable liability on affected status
conclusion: The framework uses the Pearson-Aitken selection formula to obtain conditional liability moments for deriving AUC.
scope: Moment calculation used in the binormal approximation
span: By the Pearson-Aitken (PA) formula [11], [12], we can estimate the mean and variance of the liability conditioned on the affection status and derive the AUC.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | Approximation of TPR, FPR, and AUC by the binormal ROC curve

assumptions: Test scores assumed normally distributed separately among affected and unaffected individuals
conclusion: The binormal approximation treats measurable-liability scores in cases and non-cases as normally distributed.
scope: Additional group-normal approximation beyond population normality
span: The binormal ROC curve is a classic example in ROC methodologies. In this model, we assume the test results are normally distributed in the affected and unaffected individuals. In our case, the test results are the measurable liability scores.

scope: Calibration is assumed rather than evaluated
span: We have assumed perfect calibration when deriving the results.

assumptions: A disease has one or a few variants with particularly large effects
conclusion: A few large-effect variants may invalidate the normal measurable-liability assumption.
span: The measured liability is assumed to be normally distributed. If we consider a number of SNPs with small effect sizes (as is the case in many complex diseases), the normal assumption is usually acceptable. However, if a disease has one or a few variants with particularly large effects, the normal assumption may not hold.

objects: K; Vm; uncertainty of predictive metrics
assumptions: Disease probability and explained variance are estimated quantities
conclusion: The study does not account for variability in predictive metrics induced by uncertainty in disease probability and variance explained.
scope: Particular caution when inputs come from small samples
span: We have not considered the variability of the predictive metrics in this study. It should be noted that the disease probability and the variance explained by known variants are both subject to variations, and so will be the predictive metrics derived from these two quantities. One should be careful in interpretation of the results if the disease probability or effect sizes of variants are estimated from small sample sizes.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | Areas not addressed

objects: ROC optimality; predicted disease risk; liability score
assumptions: Risks correctly specified by the most appropriate model; monotone risk ranking
conclusion: The authors state that the ROC constructed from predicted risk or its equivalent liability ranking is optimal, with practical optimality conditional on correct risk specification.
scope: Model-conditional ROC optimality; no unconditional empirical guarantee
span: In our methodology, construction of the ROC curves (and AUC) are all based on the actual predicted risks, or equivalently the liability score, which is a monotone increasing function of the actual risks. As a result, the ROC curve produced by our method should be optimal by definition. In practice, the “optimality” will depend on whether the risks are specified correctly by the most appropriate model.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | A note on the optimality of the ROC curve

assumptions: Risk score is monotone in likelihood ratio
conclusion: Risk-score ROC construction is presented as an alternative to Lu and Elston likelihood-ratio ROC construction.
span: Another method to construct the optimal ROC curve is simply to use the risk score function or the predicted probability of disease, Pr(disease| test result). This method is perhaps less recognized and has not been mentioned in Lu and Elston [4]. It has been shown that the risk score is a monotone increasing function of likelihood ratios, and therefore also gives the optimal ROC curve [23].
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | A note on the optimality of the ROC curve

objects: Liability threshold; binormal AUC approximation; heritability
assumptions: Wray et al. 2010 liability-threshold maximum-AUC setting
conclusion: The authors describe Wray et al. 2010 maximum-AUC approximation as similar to their binormal ROC approximation.
scope: Approximation-formula similarity only; equivalence of the entire frameworks is not asserted
span: Their study is also based on a liability threshold model, and they have derived an analytic formula to approximate the maximum AUC achieved when all genetic loci are found (at heritability or at fractions of it). Their formula described is similar to ours under the section on approximation of AUC by the binormal ROC curve.

objects: Predictiveness curve; absolute disease risk; risk percentile
assumptions: Liability and absolute risk are monotonically related
conclusion: The framework constructs the Pepe et al. predictiveness curve by plotting predicted absolute risk against risk percentile.
scope: Predictiveness curve as an existing visualization within the framework
span: The predictiveness curve, first proposed by Pepe et al. [7], is a useful way to visualize the predictive power of a test and the distribution of risk in the population. This curve is constructed by plotting the predicted absolute disease risks against the percentiles of the absolute risks, or transposition of the cdf curve. Since the measurable liability has a monotonic relationship with the predicted absolute risk (i.e. a higher measurable liability always leads to a higher risk), the percentiles of the measurable liability can also be used.
location: liability_threshold_model | journal OA version (Europe PMC JATS) | The predictiveness curve
